Ex Opere Operato
eks OP-eh-ray oh-peh-RAH-toh
Latin phrase (theological, historical)
Latin, "by the work worked"; the Roman doctrine that the sacraments confer grace by the performance of the rite itself.

📖 Biblical Definition

Ex opere operato is the Roman doctrine that the sacraments confer grace simply by the performance of the rite—by the work worked—apart from the faith of the recipient, so long as no positive obstacle is placed in the way. Against this the Reformed church confesses that the sacraments are signs and seals of the covenant of grace, profitable not by any power in themselves nor in him who administers them, but by the working of the Holy Ghost and the blessing of Christ in those who by faith receive them. The error of the Roman view is that it severs grace from faith and lodges it in the mechanical operation of the ritual, as though the washing of water or the eating of bread could of itself convey saving benefit to an unbelieving heart. But Scripture everywhere binds the blessing of the ordinances to faith. The word preached did not profit Israel, not being mixed with faith in them that heard it; without faith it is impossible to please God; and the just shall live by faith. The sacraments preach the same gospel to the eye that the Word preaches to the ear, and like the Word they profit only where the Spirit gives faith to embrace the Christ they set forth. To make them work automatically is to overthrow justification by faith alone, to feed presumption, and to lull the unconverted into trusting a rite rather than the Redeemer. The Reformed conviction stands: no ordinance saves the faithless; grace is received by faith, and the sacraments seal to believers the very righteousness already theirs in Christ.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Ex opere operato is the Roman doctrine that sacraments confer grace by the act itself, which the Reformed rebut from sola fide.

EX OPERE OPERATO, Latin phrase. "By the work worked."

The Roman doctrine that the sacraments confer grace through the performance of the rite itself.

Held to operate apart from the recipient's faith, provided no obstacle is placed in the way.

Rebutted by the Reformed insistence that the ordinances profit only believers through the Spirit.

Scripture binds blessing to faith: "The word preached did not profit them, not being mixed with faith in them that heard it" (Hebrews 4:2).

📖 Key Scripture

Heb 4:2 — "For unto us was the gospel preached, as well as unto them: but the word preached did not profit them, not being mixed with faith in them that heard it."

Heb 11:6 — "But without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him."

Rom 4:11 — "And he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith which he had yet being uncircumcised."

Hab 2:4 — "Behold, his soul which is lifted up is not upright in him: but the just shall live by his faith."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Rome teaches that the sacraments confer grace by the act itself, severing grace from faith.

expand to see more

The Roman doctrine of ex opere operato teaches that the sacraments convey grace by the very working of the rite, independent of the recipient's faith, so long as he sets up no bar against it. This lodges saving benefit in the mechanism of the ceremony rather than in the Christ it signifies, and it makes the priest's performance the channel of grace. The practical fruit is presumption: multitudes rest on having been baptized and having received the host, while their hearts remain unrenewed, trusting the ritual instead of the Redeemer.

The Reformed rebuttal flows from justification by faith alone. Abraham received circumcision as a seal of the righteousness of the faith he already had; the sacraments seal what faith receives, they do not create grace where faith is absent. Hebrews declares the Word unprofitable when not mixed with faith, and without faith it is impossible to please God. The just shall live by faith—not by a work worked upon him. Thus the ordinances are means the Spirit blesses to believers, never automatic conduits to the unbelieving. To recover the truth is to send sinners not to the rite but to Christ, embraced by faith alone.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The rebuttal rests on the Scriptures that bind the blessing of all ordinances to faith.

expand to see more

Hebrews 4:2 declares the preached Word unprofitable when not mixed with faith.

Hebrews 11:6 teaches that without faith it is impossible to please God.

Romans 4:11 makes circumcision a seal of a righteousness already received by faith.

Habakkuk 2:4 grounds life in faith: the just shall live by his faith.

The 1689 Confession denies any virtue in the sacraments apart from the Spirit's work in believers.

Usage

"Used to name the Roman view: "Rome holds the sacraments work ex opere operato.""

"Used in rebuttal: "ex opere operato severs grace from faith.""

"Used to warn against presumption: "an ex opere operato religion trusts the rite, not Christ.""
